My cousin had to have his tonsils removed a few years ago. The resulting bill, prior to what the insurance covered was $125,000. That is nearly 3 times the average salary, before taxes, of the average american ($43,000.)

If a hospital billed the average american an amount of $125,000, they would likely never see their money, or they would never see an appreciable amount throughout the life of the payment.

It is the first or second chapter of any 1st year undergraduate economics textbook: the Willingness and Able Principle. An individual who makes 43k a year neither has the means nor the willingness to be able to pay off a 6 figure bill while paying all other amenities and taxes.

An insurance company however, that makes hundreds of millions if not billions in revenue a year can. A hospital is not really billing the individual, but the insurance company. And because an insurance company is willing and able to pay off a 6 figure procedure, if not more, a hospital can charge whatever it wants, all in the name of profit.

Thus all insurance companies inflate the prices of the commodities or procedures that they insure, by aggregating its clients payments into 9-10 figure pools.

If there were no insurance companies and service providers billed the individual directly, service providers would be forced to adjust their payments so that they would see appreciable payments.
